topics.label: Lecture framing: cancer evolution, cell of origin and microenvironment
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic welcomes the audience, frames the lecture's subject and states its learning aims rather than developing a substantive argument.

topics.label: Mutation accumulation and clonal selection in cancer evolution
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics show how accumulating genetic changes can give clones a selective advantage and contribute to cancer development.

topics.label: Epigenetic disruption as a driver of tumor development
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how transient changes to the epigenetic landscape can alter transcription and contribute to tumor development.

topics.label: Stemness, cell of origin and tumor hierarchy
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine whether cancer growth follows a stem-like hierarchy, using leukemia and intestinal tumor models to explore the cells that can initiate or propagate tumors.

topics.label: Inflammation-induced stemness in cancer initiation
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics show how inflammatory signals can provide conditions that let mutated cells acquire stem-like properties and develop into tumors.

topics.label: Microenvironmental support of established tumors and therapeutic targeting
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains that established tumors can depend on supportive cells in their microenvironment and describes targeting that support as a therapeutic strategy.

topics.label: Single-cell and spatial approaches to studying cancer evolution
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic describes sequencing and spatial methods for examining tumor-cell states and their interactions within tissue.

topics.label: An integrated evolutionary model of cancer development
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic brings together mutations, cell properties and environmental conditions to explain how their interaction can enable malignant growth.

topics.label: Lecture close: cancer therapy next
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic ends the lecture and points the audience to the subject of the next lecture.
